title: 6 Best Hookaroons for Firewood in 2026: Length Matters Most
metaDescription: The Fiskars 28-inch is the best hookaroon for firewood for most homeowners. 6 hookaroons and pickaroons compared by length, head and handle material.
h1: The 6 Best Hookaroons for Firewood in 2026
intro:
The best hookaroon for firewood for most homeowners is the Fiskars 28-inch: long enough to pick rounds off the ground from a near-upright stance, short enough to work beside a splitter, with a hardened steel head on a weatherproof composite handle.

A hookaroon is the cheapest back-saver in the firewood workflow. The hard part of processing wood is not splitting it; it is bending over hundreds of times to grab rounds, feed the splitter and toss splits. Below are six picks, from a traditional hickory tool to an aluminum lightweight and a 3-in-1 multitool, followed by how to choose a length, use one safely and keep the point sharp.
quickAnswer: Buy the Fiskars 28-inch hookaroon if you want one tool for splitting and stacking. Choose the Council Tool for a forged head on a replaceable hickory handle, the LogRite for the lightest aluminum handle, or the LogOX 3-in-1 if you also need to roll and lift logs while bucking. For most people, a length in the upper 20 inches is the right single choice.

Length decides more than brand. A tool in the 26- to 30-inch range reaches rounds on the ground without deep bending and still works at the splitter, so it is the best single buy. Heavy users often add a short 15- to 18-inch pickaroon for fast work right at the beam.

After length, look at the point and the handle. A slim, hardened point sets with a light swing; a blunt or soft one glances off. Pick the handle material by how you store tools: composite and aluminum shrug off weather, while hickory feels best but needs oil and a dry place to hang.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Hookaroons for Firewood in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
These picks are based on maker details such as overall length, handle material, head construction and warranty, plus how each design handles the jobs homeowners do most: pulling rounds, feeding a splitter and stacking. Owner feedback patterns were weighed too. Confirm the exact length of any listing before you buy, since several brands sell more than one size.

### Best Overall: Fiskars 28-Inch Hookaroon

The Fiskars 28-inch is the easiest recommendation for a homeowner firewood setup. At 28 inches it reaches rounds lying on the ground and tosses splits onto a pile without deep bending, yet it stays short enough to swing in the tight space beside a splitter.

Fiskars pairs a hardened steel head with a composite handle that resists weather and never needs the oiling a wood handle does, and a textured grip helps when your gloves are wet. It is widely sold at a middle-of-the-market price. Owners commonly praise how readily the point bites into rounds and how the curve helps pull wood toward you.

It is not a log-rolling tool; very large logs call for a cant hook. A composite handle also cannot be swapped out like a wood one if it ever fails. Keep the tip sharp and store it so the point cannot catch anyone.

**Pros:** length works for ground pickup and stacking; weatherproof composite handle; hardened head bites easily; widely available.

**Cons:** not for rolling big logs; handle is not replaceable; point needs occasional touch-ups.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Fiskars+28+inch+hookaroon&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Traditional Build: Council Tool Hookaroon

Council Tool is an American maker known for forged axes and forestry tools, and its hookaroon follows that tradition with a forged steel head on a hickory handle. Hickory is strong and soaks up shock, so it stays comfortable through a long session, and a damaged handle can be replaced instead of throwing out the tool.

The forged head holds a point and takes a file easily. The wood needs some care: a coat of boiled linseed oil now and then, and storage out of the rain. Many owners prefer the feel and balance of hickory over composite, and this is the pick for anyone searching for a wood-handle hookaroon that can be kept going for decades. Council Tool has offered different handle lengths over time, so check the one listed.

**Pros:** forged steel head; shock-absorbing hickory; replaceable handle; American forestry heritage.

**Cons:** handle needs periodic oil; must be stored dry; usually costs more than composite models.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Council+Tool+hookaroon&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Brand Ecosystem: Husqvarna Hookaroon

Husqvarna sells a hookaroon in its forestry accessory line, next to its chainsaws, splitting axes and log tongs. It uses a hardened steel head with a curved point shaped to grab rounds and splits, and it is sold by Husqvarna dealers and many retailers that carry its saws, which makes it a convenient add-on when you are buying a saw.

It is a straightforward, durable tool rather than a specialized one. Husqvarna's forestry range includes both short pickaroon-style tools and longer hookaroons, so check the length: short for working at the splitter, long for stacking from the ground. Like any steel head, it benefits from a file touch-up and a light coat of oil to keep rust off the point.

**Pros:** hardened head with curved point; sold alongside Husqvarna saws; durable design; dealer availability.

**Cons:** several lengths in the line; not specialized for large logs; price varies by dealer.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Husqvarna+hookaroon&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Lightweight: LogRite Hookaroon

LogRite is best known for aluminum-handled cant hooks and peaveys, and its hookaroon applies the same idea: a light, strong aluminum handle with a steel hook. The weight savings add up over a full day of feeding a splitter and stacking, and aluminum never rots or swells in wet weather.

LogRite has a loyal following among people who process a lot of wood and want American-built gear. The trade-offs are a higher price than mass-market tools and a different feel from hickory; some users find aluminum transmits more vibration on impact, and it feels cold in winter, which a good glove fixes. If you already own a LogRite cant hook, this is its natural partner.

**Pros:** light aluminum handle reduces fatigue; will not rot or swell; strong reputation with heavy users; pairs with LogRite cant hooks.

**Cons:** priced above mass-market models; aluminum feels different from wood; less common in big-box stores.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=LogRite+hookaroon&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Dealer Pick: Stihl Hookaroon

Stihl offers a hookaroon in its forestry tool lineup, sold through the same dealers as its chainsaws. The head is designed to grab and pull rounds, and the handle gives enough reach to move and stack wood with less bending. It is a practical, durable tool without exotic features.

Buying from a Stihl dealer makes sense if you are already there for a saw, chain or bar oil, and dealers can advise on length and show you how to set and free the point safely, which helps first-time users. Many shoppers search for a Stihl pickaroon; lineup and handle length vary by region, so confirm the exact version your dealer stocks.

**Pros:** sold through Stihl dealers; durable head for pulling rounds; easy add-on to a saw purchase; practical stacking length.

**Cons:** lineup varies by region; mostly dealer-only; no standout features over rivals.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Stihl+hookaroon&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Multi-Tool: LogOX 3-in-1 Forestry Multitool

The LogOX is not a pure hookaroon. It is a modular forestry tool that combines a hookaroon-style tine with a cant hook and a log jack on a steel frame, with a handle you reconfigure for each job. That makes it the pick for heavy logs: you can roll a log for bucking, lift it so the chain stays out of the dirt, and carry rounds with two hands instead of bending.

It is heavier and costs more than a simple hookaroon, and if all you do is feed a splitter and stack, a light dedicated tool is faster. For someone cutting trees on their own property, though, it can replace two or three tools and makes handling big logs safer. Read the instructions for each configuration before using it.

**Pros:** hookaroon, cant hook and log jack in one; keeps the chain out of dirt; helps roll and carry large logs; replaces several tools.

**Cons:** heavier than a dedicated hookaroon; higher price; slower for simple stacking.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=LogOX+3-in-1+forestry+multitool&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: What Is a Hookaroon Used For?
sections.body:
A hookaroon is used to grab, drag, lift, flip and toss firewood rounds and splits without bending over or putting your hands near rough bark and splinters. It is a curved, pointed steel spike on a handle, usually about 15 to 30 inches long. You swing the point lightly into the wood, then move the piece with the handle.

### The jobs it does best

- Pulling rounds off a pile and dragging them to the splitter
- Positioning the next round on the splitter beam
- Pulling split halves off the beam so your hands stay away from the wedge
- Sorting splits and tossing them onto the stack or into a cart

### How it fits with other log tools

| Tool | Main job | When to choose it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hookaroon or pickaroon | Grab, drag and toss rounds and splits | Splitting and stacking firewood |
| Cant hook | Roll and turn logs on the ground | Bucking downed trees into rounds |
| Peavey | Roll logs, with a spiked tip for prying | Larger logs and landing work |
| Log tongs | Carry and drag logs | Moving logs to the bucking area |

A cant hook and peavey have long handles and a hinged hook for rolling logs while you buck them with a chainsaw. They do not replace a hookaroon, and a hookaroon does not replace them. Most people who cut their own trees end up owning both, or a combined tool like the LogOX. If you split with a machine, our [log splitter guide](/best-log-splitter/) covers the other half of the job.

sections.heading: Hookaroon vs Pickaroon: What Is the Difference?
sections.body:
The names are often used for the same tool. Where people separate them, a pickaroon tends to have a shorter, more axe-like head with a straighter spike, while a hookaroon has a more pronounced curve for pulling. Many makers simply choose one name, so do not shop by the label.

### What actually matters

Two things decide how the tool works: overall length and point shape. A straighter spike drives in and pulls out easily but holds less securely when you lift. A stronger curve grips better when you pull a round toward you or lift a split, but it takes a small twist to free.

### Short pickaroon, long hookaroon

In practice, many heavy users keep a short pickaroon, about 15 to 18 inches, at the splitter for quick one-handed moves, and a longer hookaroon in the upper 20s for the pile and the stack. If you search for the best pickaroon for firewood and only want one tool, choose by length first and treat the name as a detail.

sections.heading: What Length Hookaroon Is Best?
sections.body:
For most homeowners, a hookaroon of about 26 to 30 inches is the best single choice, which is why 28-inch tools like the Fiskars are so popular. That length reaches rounds on the ground from a near-upright stance and still works at the splitter.

| Length | Best use |
| --- | --- |
| 15-18 in | Quick, one-handed work at the splitter |
| 24-26 in | Balanced reach and control |
| 28-30 in | Ground pickup, dragging and stacking |
| Two tools | Common setup for heavy users |

### Short tools

Short tools are nimble right at the splitter, where you move splits from the beam to a pile a few feet away. They are easy to control one-handed, but you bend more to reach rounds on the ground.

### Long tools

Long tools reach the ground from a standing posture, so they are better for pulling rounds off a pile, dragging them to the splitter and stacking low rows. They need a little more room to swing.

### Height and weight

Taller users gain the most from a longer handle. If several people will use it, buy the longer tool; choking up on a long handle is easier than stretching a short one. A long handle with a heavy forged head sets the point with more momentum but tires the arms faster, so try a few practice swings or choose a lighter handle material if you work for hours at a time.

sections.heading: What Makes a Good Hookaroon Head and Point?
sections.body:
A good hookaroon has a slim, sharp, hardened steel point that sets with a light swing and comes out with a small twist, on a head that is firmly fixed to the handle. The point does nearly all the work.

### Point shape

A slim tip penetrates bark and end grain easily, while a blunt tip glances off and makes you swing harder, which is tiring and less safe. A pronounced curve helps you pull wood toward you and hold it while lifting. Avoid exaggerated, hooked tips that are hard to free; yanking on a stuck tool is how people strain their backs and lose their footing.

### Steel and heat treatment

Forged, hardened heads hold a point and resist bending, which is why the Council Tool, Fiskars and Husqvarna heads are described as forged or hardened. Soft or poorly treated heads dull or bend after hitting a knot or a stone.

### Attachment

On wood handles, look for a secure wedge or fastening. On composite and aluminum handles, the head should be bonded or bolted solidly. A loose head can fly off mid-swing.

### Extras

Some heads add a flat poll or hammer face for tapping a wedge or knocking a split loose, and a few add a small blade. These extras add weight but can earn their keep at the woodpile.

sections.heading: Wood Handle, Composite or Aluminum Hookaroon?
sections.body:
Choose hickory for feel and a replaceable handle, composite for low upkeep at a fair price, and aluminum for the lightest tool on long days. Each works; the right one depends on how you store your tools.

### Hickory

Hickory is the traditional choice because it is strong, flexible and absorbs shock. A damaged wood handle can be replaced, so the head can outlive several handles. The trade-off is care: keep it out of the rain, wipe it down when wet and rub in boiled linseed oil a few times a year to stop it drying and cracking. The Council Tool is the wood-handle pick here.

### Composite and fiberglass

Composite handles ignore weather, need no oil and generally resist breaking from an overstrike. They suit owners who leave tools near the woodpile. They feel a little different in the hand and cannot easily be replaced if they fail. The Fiskars uses one.

### Aluminum

Aluminum is the lightest option and never rots or swells, which is why it shows up on premium tools like the LogRite. Some users find it transmits more vibration or feels cold in winter; a good glove handles both.

### Grip

Whatever the material, choose a grip that works with gloves, since you should always wear them at the woodpile. Texture or rubber helps when the handle is wet.

sections.heading: How Do You Use a Hookaroon Safely?
sections.body:
Set the point with a short, controlled swing into the side or end grain a few inches from the edge, then move the wood with your legs and core rather than your lower back. Never use it near a moving splitter ram.

### Basic moves

- **Drag a round:** set the point and walk backward slowly, watching your footing.
- **Flip a round onto its end:** set the point near the top edge and pull up and toward you.
- **Toss a split:** set the point near the center of gravity, lift slightly and release smoothly toward the pile, never toward people or pets.
- **Free the point:** rock it gently in line with the curve. Prying sideways bends points and snaps wood handles.

### At the splitter

Use the hookaroon to pull halves off the beam and to position the next round, which keeps your hands farther from the wedge. Wait for the ram to stop or retract before you set the point; a tool caught by a moving ram can be wrenched toward you.

### Gear and footing

Wear sturdy gloves, eye protection and boots with protective toes, since chips fly and dropped rounds crush toes. Keep a clear swing area, plant your feet wide and set the point to the side of your stance, never toward your feet. Avoid ice and wet slopes, and keep bark and small splits raked up so you do not trip.

### A back-friendly workflow

Buck logs near where you split them, drag rounds to the splitter instead of carrying them, and set a cart or wheelbarrow at waist height beside the stack. If you haul wood with a machine, our [compact tractor guide](/best-compact-tractor/) covers loaders and attachments, and a [weed eater](/best-weed-eater/) keeps grass down around the pile so rodents stay away.

sections.heading: How Do You Sharpen and Store a Hookaroon?
sections.body:
Touch up the point with a mill file, keep the head oiled and store the tool point-to-the-wall or covered. A sharp point sets with a light swing; a dull one forces you to swing harder.

### Sharpening

File toward the tip, following the existing profile, and keep the point slim and symmetrical. Avoid a bench grinder unless you can keep the steel cool, because overheating can ruin the temper and soften the point. Do not use a bent point, which can slip out of the wood without warning.

### Cleaning and rust

Wipe sap and dirt off the head after use and give it a light coat of oil. Rust weakens the point over time and makes it harder to set.

### Handle care

Wipe moisture off wood handles after use and oil them a few times a year. Do not leave hickory lying in wet grass or snow, which swells the wood and loosens the head. Composite and aluminum need only a wipe.

### Storage

Hang the tool with the point facing the wall, or cover the point with a sheath or a split piece of hose. A hookaroon left in the grass or leaning on a stack is easy to step on or knock over, so keep it under cover and out of reach of children.

sections.heading: Who Makes the Best Hookaroons?
sections.body:
Fiskars, Council Tool, LogRite, Husqvarna and Stihl make the hookaroons most often recommended for firewood, and LogOX makes the best-known multitool. The best maker for you depends on what you value.

### By priority

- **Best all-round value:** Fiskars, for a 28-inch tool with a weatherproof handle at a mid-market price.
- **Longest-lived traditional tool:** Council Tool, for a forged head on replaceable hickory.
- **Lightest for long days:** LogRite, with its aluminum handle.
- **Buying with a saw:** Husqvarna or Stihl, through the same dealer.
- **Cutting your own trees:** LogOX, which adds cant hook and log jack functions.

### Do you need one at all?

If you split your own wood, especially with a machine, a hookaroon is one of the best values in the whole process. If you buy split firewood and only stack it, it is optional, though many owners still use one to load a wheelbarrow and rearrange stacks. If you buck your own trees, pair it with a cant hook or choose a multitool.

Spend on a good point, a length suited to your height and setup, and a handle material that fits how you store tools. Those three choices matter far more than the name on the head. And take breaks: most strains at the woodpile happen late in a long session, when form slips. Pair the hookaroon with a well-matched [log splitter](/best-log-splitter/) and the whole job gets easier on your back.

mistakes.title: Buying too short a tool
mistakes.body: Short tools are quick at the splitter but make you bend to reach rounds on the ground, which defeats much of the point. Unless you work only at waist height, choose a hookaroon in the upper 20-inch range, or own a short and a long one.

mistakes.title: Swinging too hard
mistakes.body: A sharp point needs only a light swing. Big overhead strikes waste energy, bury the point too deep and raise the chance of glancing off into your leg or foot. Use a short, controlled motion and keep the point sharp.

mistakes.title: Reaching in while the splitter ram moves
mistakes.body: Setting a hookaroon near a moving ram is as dangerous as reaching in with your hand, because the tool can be caught and wrenched toward you. Wait until the ram stops or fully retracts before you clear or position wood.

mistakes.title: Prying with the point
mistakes.body: Using a hookaroon as a pry bar bends points and breaks handles, especially wood ones. Free a stuck point by rocking it in line with the curve, and leave rolling and prying logs to a cant hook or peavey.

mistakes.title: Leaving it lying in the grass
mistakes.body: A hookaroon left point-up in grass or leaves is easy to step on, and wood handles left wet swell and loosen. Hang it point-to-the-wall or cover the point, under cover and out of reach of children.

faqs.q: What is the best hookaroon for firewood?
faqs.a: The Fiskars 28-inch hookaroon is the best choice for most firewood users. Its length reaches rounds on the ground from a near-upright stance and still works beside a splitter, and it pairs a hardened steel head with a weatherproof composite handle. For a wood handle, choose the Council Tool; for the lightest tool, the LogRite.

Fiskars, Council Tool, LogRite, Husqvarna and Stihl make the most recommended hookaroons. Fiskars leads on value with its 28-inch composite tool, Council Tool on traditional forged-and-hickory construction, and LogRite on light aluminum handles. Husqvarna and Stihl are convenient if you buy saws from their dealers, and LogOX makes the leading 3-in-1 multitool.

faqs.q: Is a 28-inch hookaroon the right length?
faqs.a: Yes, for most homeowners. A 28-inch hookaroon reaches rounds on the ground from a near-upright stance, works at the splitter and handles stacking, so it is the best single length. The same checks apply to any 28-inch pickaroon you are comparing: a slim hardened point, a secure head and a handle that grips well with gloves.

faqs.q: What is the best pickaroon for heavy logs?
faqs.a: For heavy logs, the LogOX 3-in-1 is the better tool, because it adds cant hook and log jack functions that roll and lift logs a pickaroon cannot. A hookaroon or pickaroon is built for rounds and splits, not whole logs. For large rounds, choose a long, forged-head tool like the Council Tool and drag rather than lift.

faqs.q: Is a pickaroon different from a hookaroon?
faqs.a: Mostly in name. Where people separate them, a pickaroon has a shorter, more axe-like head with a straighter spike, and a hookaroon has a more pronounced curve for pulling. Makers use both names for similar tools, so judge any model by its overall length and point shape rather than by the label on the listing.

faqs.q: Is a wood handle hookaroon better?
faqs.a: A wood handle is better for feel and long life, not for low upkeep. Hickory absorbs shock and can be replaced when damaged, so the forged head can outlast several handles, as on the Council Tool. It needs boiled linseed oil a few times a year and dry storage. Composite and aluminum handles need almost no care.

faqs.q: Do I still need a cant hook if I own a hookaroon?
faqs.a: Yes, if you buck your own logs. A cant hook has a long handle and a hinged hook for rolling logs on the ground while you cut them into rounds; a hookaroon moves rounds and splits. They do different jobs. If you want one tool that does both, the LogOX 3-in-1 combines a hookaroon tine, cant hook and log jack.

bottomLine: For most people who split and stack their own firewood, the Fiskars 28-inch hookaroon is the tool to buy: the right length for ground pickup and splitter work, a hardened steel point and a handle that ignores the weather. Choose the Council Tool if you want forged steel on replaceable hickory, the LogRite if you work long days and want the lightest handle, Husqvarna or Stihl if you are already at their dealer, and the LogOX if you also roll and lift whole logs. Whatever you buy, keep the point sharp, swing lightly, stay clear of a moving splitter ram and hang the tool point-to-the-wall.
